newsitem.title: UKRAINE: FEATURE - Ukraine farm takes first steps to land ownership.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Ukraine farm takes first steps to land ownership.

text.p: A handful of farmers are pushing ahead with plans to transform Ukraine's crumbling state-run farm sector into a model of private enterprise, despite bureaucratic inertia and the absence of a clear legal framework.

A landmark occasion here typified the spirit behind the initiative, when kerchiefed women and fur-hatted men filled the farm hall to celebrate becoming land-owners, a novelty in this former Soviet republic still in the early stages of economic reform.
"A free man is a free man, who can work for himself, his family and therefore his country," smiled Volodymyr Hladun.

Hladun, celebrating the division of Oktyabr into the Pryvilne (Freedom) and Troyanda (Rose) farms as part of the land reform project, is now the head of Pryvilne farm, located in the eastern Donetsk region best known for heavy industry and coal mines.

The Oktyabr farm is typical of its kind, with 4,500 hectares of land under cultivation in a gently rolling landscape punctuated by a brick school, a large cattle barn, and a nearby village with houses and neatly-swept yards.
"Private land ownership can conquer all," said Hladun.
PRIVATE LAND OWNERSHIP STILL NOT LEGAL
More than five years after independence and more than two since Ukraine launched its economic reform programme, private land ownership has still not been made legal in this country of 51 million.
The farm sector is still dominated by 18-20,000 collective agricultural enterprises (CAEs) and a much smaller number of remaining state-run collectives.

But a handful of farmers, under a project sponsored by the British Know-How Fund and the International Finance Corporation (IFC), the World Bank's private investment arm, have used a series of government declarations and motions sanctioning the idea of land ownership to their advantage.

"Our project is what we call 'legally defensible' in the existing framework of Ukrainian laws," said Maciej Gadamski, the IFC project manager of the land privatisation and farm reorganisation project, first started in Russia in 1992.
KUCHMA STRESSES NEED FOR LAND REFORM
President Leonid Kuchma has stressed the need for land reform and the development of a market in land if Ukraine is to prove it is serious about economic reforms.

"Now that we stand firmly on the road of market reform we must clearly accept the fact that a market economy without a land market does not exist and cannot exist," Kuchma told Ukrainians in a recent televised broadcast.

But conservative deputies have said repeatedly that selling land would strip Ukraine of its wealth. Their opposition has delayed the passage of a law legalising the sale of land, and made ineffective the clause guaranteeing private land ownership in the new constitution passed last year.

Gadamski said the Donetsk region was chosen for the reform project not only because it produces a good cross-section of Ukraine's crops, such as grain, sunflowers, sugar beet and cereal, but also because there is political support here.

Once Oktyabr was divided into two farms, its land and assets were distributed to the farm workers in the hope that this would boost production. "Productivity is the ultimate goal for any enterprise in this country," Gadamski said.
IFC studies have shown such farms increase their productivity compared with neighbouring state farms and CAEs, which continue to rely heavily on government funds for supplies, fuel and machinery.

The government has adopted a go-slow approach to dismantling the farms, fearing output would collapse without the state-run collective system forcibly imposed by Soviet leader Josef Stalin in the 1930s.
Some 30,000 private farmers, who face a six-year moratorium on the sale of land, have had little support from the cash-strapped government.

Productivity on Soviet-era farms, which were inefficient to begin with, has eroded even more since independence, mainly because of shortages of fertilisers and machine parts, although last year's record low grain crop of 24.5 million tonnes was blamed on drought.
NOT ALL FARMERS WANT TO END COLLECTIVE FARM SYSTEM

Each farm re-organisation has seen members of collectives voting for leaders, meetings to distribute assets like tractors, buildings and abattoirs, and decisions on whether to take over the land now or later.
But not every newly-declared land owner has embraced change.

Kateryna Bobenko said she and her husband returned their 8.9 hectares of land to the Troyanda farm for cultivation, receiving grain, oil, milk and hay in exchange, and may claim it back in a year or two.

"Somehow I think it was better to be in the kolhosp," she said, referring to the old system that is all that several generations of farmers have known. "But we hope this will be better," she added doubtfully.
Stalin's forced collectivisation produced an artificial famine that killed an estimated seven million Ukrainians who opposed it.
"It takes a while to get out of the existing mould that was here for 70 years or so," Gadamski said.

"The most important goal is to allow and assist people in realising their right to assets and land. People can make a choice," he said. "We will reach the breaking point when they start receiving dividends," he added.
Gadamski said other regions are also pushing through their own farm re-organisations, and the IFC plans to launch similar projects in other parts of the country.
